a larger momentum, because it is heavier.
p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.explanation: Momentum conservation gives equal and opposite momenta ($p$). Kinetic energy is $p^2/2m$, so the light bullet carries nearly all the kinetic energy and the heavy rifle very little.

p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.prompt: An explosion tears a stationary object into pieces with very large internal forces. Why is the total momentum of the pieces still zero?
options: Because Newton's laws do not apply to explosions, so a separate rule fixes the momentum at zero.
Because the internal forces are so large that they average to zero over the short time of the blast.
Because the pieces all end up with equal masses, so their momenta must cancel in pairs.
Internal forces cancel in equal and opposite pairs; only external forces change the total momentum.
p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.explanation: For each pair of particles $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$ (third law), so the sum of internal forces is zero and $d\vec P/dt = \vec F_{ext}$. If no external force acts, the total momentum is constant.

p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.prompt: Explain how Newton's third law leads to conservation of total momentum for an isolated system, and use it to say why a stationary nucleus that decays into two fragments sends them off in opposite directions.
p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.rubric: Full credit: internal forces are equal and opposite so $d(\vec p_1+\vec p_2)/dt = 0$; the total momentum stays at its initial value (zero for the nucleus at rest), so $\vec p_1 = -\vec p_2$: opposite directions, equal magnitudes (the lighter one is faster).
p1-l036-momentum-conservation-explosions.modelAnswer: For two interacting bodies $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$, so $d\vec p_1/dt + d\vec p_2/dt = 0$ and total momentum is constant. A nucleus at rest starts with zero momentum, so the fragments must have equal and opposite momenta: opposite directions, with the lighter fragment moving faster. This works without knowing anything about the forces involved.

p1-l037-collisions-1d.prompt: A billiard ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on in a perfectly elastic 1D collision. Afterwards,
options: both balls move forward, each with half of the original speed, sharing the motion equally.
the first ball stops and the second moves off at the first ball's original speed.
the first ball rebounds backward while the second ball moves forward at the same speed.
both balls come to rest, because the momentum of one ball is shared between them and cancels.
p1-l037-collisions-1d.explanation: For equal masses, momentum and energy conservation give $v_{1f} = 0$, $v_{2f} = v_{1i}$: the balls exchange velocities. Check: $K$ is unchanged and $p$ is unchanged.

p1-l037-collisions-1d.prompt: A 2 kg cart rolling at 6 m/s collides and sticks to a 4 kg cart at rest. Which quantity is conserved in this perfectly inelastic collision?
options: Total momentum only; the kinetic energy that disappears goes into heat and deformation.
Total kinetic energy only, because the carts stay together and nothing is lost to the surroundings.
Both total momentum and total kinetic energy, as in every collision with no external force.
Neither, because the carts stick together and the combined cart starts from a new state.
p1-l037-collisions-1d.explanation: No external horizontal force acts, so total momentum is conserved ($12 = 6v'$ gives $v' = 2$ m/s). The kinetic energy drops from 36 J to 12 J; the missing energy appears as heat and deformation.

p1-l037-collisions-1d.prompt: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s collides and sticks to a 4.0 kg cart at rest. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy is lost? Give the answer as a decimal fraction.
p1-l037-collisions-1d.explanation: $v' = (2)(6)/6 = 2$ m/s; $K_i = 36$ J, $K_f = 12$ J, so $2/3 \approx 0.667$ of the energy is lost. In general the lost fraction is $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ for a target initially at rest.

p1-l037-collisions-1d.prompt: In a perfectly inelastic collision kinetic energy is lost, yet momentum is conserved. Explain where the energy goes, why momentum is still conserved, and what fixes the fraction of kinetic energy lost.
p1-l037-collisions-1d.rubric: Full credit requires: internal forces (deformation, heat, sound) convert kinetic energy to other forms; momentum is conserved because the internal forces are equal and opposite and there is no net external impulse; the fraction lost depends on the mass ratio (and is largest relative to initial K when the masses are comparable).
p1-l037-collisions-1d.modelAnswer: The kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat and sound through internal forces. Those forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law) and there is no external impulse, so total momentum is unchanged. The lost fraction is set by the masses: $K_{lost}/K_i = m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ for a stationary target.

p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.prompt: In a scattering experiment where a small ball hits a larger fixed sphere (a billiard-ball model of molecular collisions), how does the deflection angle depend on the impact parameter $b$ (the perpendicular offset of the incoming line from the centre)?
options: The deflection is the same for every impact parameter, since it is set only by the target's size.
A head-on hit gives no deflection at all, while a large $b$ gives strong backscatter.
Deflection depends only on the speed of the incoming particle, not on where it strikes.
A head-on hit ($b=0$) gives the largest deflection; larger $b$ gives less, and a miss gives none.
p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.explanation: A glancing blow transfers little transverse momentum, while a head-on collision reverses the direction. Measuring the distribution of deflection angles is how we learn the size and shape of molecules in scattering experiments.

p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.prompt: A moving ball strikes an identical ball at rest in an elastic but off-centre (2D) collision. Explain why the two balls leave at right angles to each other.
p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.rubric: Full credit: momentum: $\vec v = \vec v_1' + \vec v_2'$ (equal masses); energy: $v^2 = v_1'^2 + v_2'^2$; the vector triangle with $v^2 = v_1'^2 + v_2'^2$ is a right triangle (Pythagoras), so $\vec v_1'\perp\vec v_2'$ (unless one is zero).
p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.modelAnswer: With equal masses, conservation of momentum says $\vec v = \vec v_1' + \vec v_2'$, and conservation of energy says $v^2 = v_1'^2 + v_2'^2$. Squaring the first gives $v^2 = v_1'^2 + v_2'^2 + 2\vec v_1'\cdot\vec v_2'$, so the dot product must vanish: the final velocities are perpendicular.

p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.prompt: A moving ball strikes an identical stationary ball in an elastic, off-centre collision. The first ball leaves at $30^\circ$ to its original line of motion. At what angle does the struck ball move?
options: $30^\circ$ from the original line, on the other side
$60^\circ$ from the original line, on the other side
$90^\circ$ from the original line, on the other side
Cannot be found without the speeds and masses
p1-l038-collisions-2d-scattering.explanation: For equal masses and an elastic collision with a stationary target, momentum and energy conservation force the outgoing velocities to be perpendicular, so the second ball leaves at $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ on the other side.

p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.prompt: In carbon monoxide the C and O nuclei are 1.128 Angstrom apart ($m_C = 12.011$ u, $m_O = 15.999$ u). How far is the centre of mass from the carbon nucleus? Give the answer in Angstrom.
p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.explanation: $x_{cm} = m_O d/(m_C+m_O) = (15.999)(1.128)/(28.010) = 0.644$ Angstrom from the carbon (measured toward oxygen). The CM lies nearer the heavier atom.

p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.prompt: A uniform circular disc of radius $R$ has a small circular hole cut out, centred a distance $R/2$ from the disc's centre. Where is the centre of mass of the remaining plate?
options: At the disc's centre, because the disc is symmetric
At the centre of the hole, where the mass was removed
On the opposite side of the disc's centre from the hole
On the same side as the hole, where there is less mass
p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.explanation: Removing a piece is like adding negative mass at the hole, so the centre of mass shifts away from the hole, to the opposite side of the original centre.

p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.prompt: Explain how symmetry lets you locate the centre of mass of a uniform rod, ring or sphere without integrating, why the centre of mass of a ring is not on the material, and when integration is unavoidable.
p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.rubric: Full credit requires: the centre of mass lies on every symmetry plane/axis of a uniform body; so the intersection (midpoint, centre) gives it; a ring's centre of mass is at its centre where there is no material; integrals are needed when there is no such symmetry or the density varies.
p1-l039-computing-center-of-mass.modelAnswer: For a uniform body, mass is distributed identically on both sides of any symmetry plane, so the centre of mass lies on it; intersecting such planes gives the midpoint of a rod or the centre of a ring or sphere. A ring's centre of mass is at its centre, in the empty hole. When the shape or density has no symmetry you must integrate $\int \vec r\,dm / M$.

p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.prompt: A spinning, tumbling hammer is thrown through the air (ignore air resistance). The path of its centre of mass is
options: a straight line, since the hammer is rigid.
a wobbly curve that depends on how it spins.
a smooth parabola, exactly as for a point mass, whatever the spin.
a parabola only if the hammer does not rotate.
p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.explanation: $\vec F_{ext} = M\vec A_{cm}$: the CM responds only to the external force (gravity here), so it follows a parabola. All the complicated tumbling is internal motion about the CM.

p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.prompt: A firework shell is moving along a parabola when it explodes into many fragments. Ignoring air resistance, the centre of mass of the fragments afterward
options: stops at the point of the explosion, because the shell's motion ends when it breaks apart.
moves in a straight line at the shell's old velocity, since the explosion adds no net push.
keeps following the original parabola until the first fragment hits the ground.
moves upward, away from the Earth, because the blast pushes all the fragments outward.
p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.explanation: The explosion's forces are internal, so they cannot change the motion of the CM; only gravity (external) acts on the system as a whole.

p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.prompt: A heavy atom (mass $M$) and a light atom (mass $m \ll M$) are bonded. The reduced mass $\mu = mM/(m+M)$ that governs their relative vibration is approximately
options: $M$, the mass of the heavier atom.
$m$, the mass of the lighter atom.
$(m+M)/2$, the average.
$\sqrt{mM}$.
p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.explanation: When $M\gg m$, $\mu \to m$: the heavy atom barely moves, so the vibration is essentially that of the light atom. For HCl the reduced mass is close to the mass of H, which is why isotope substitution of H by D shifts the frequency.

p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.prompt: Explain why the centre of mass is such a useful concept: what does $\vec F_{ext} = M\vec A_{cm}$ tell us, and how does the kinetic energy of a system of particles split up?
p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.rubric: Full credit: internal forces cancel in pairs so the whole system's total momentum changes only due to external force: CM behaves like a point mass $M$ acted on by $F_{ext}$; kinetic energy splits as $\tfrac12MV_{cm}^2$ (motion of the CM) plus internal KE relative to the CM (rotation, vibration), which for two bodies uses reduced mass.
p1-l040-center-of-mass-motion-reduced-ma.modelAnswer: Because internal forces cancel in pairs, the total momentum changes only through external forces: the CM moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted on it. The kinetic energy separates cleanly into $\tfrac12MV_{cm}^2$ plus the kinetic energy of motion relative to the CM (spin, vibration); for two bodies the latter involves the reduced mass $\mu$.

p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.prompt: How can a rocket accelerate in empty space when there is nothing to push against?
options: It cannot; rockets only work in an atmosphere, where the exhaust pushes against the air.
It pushes against the Earth's gravitational field, which acts as a medium far from the planet.
It pushes against the surrounding vacuum, which still has a small residual pressure.
It expels exhaust backward, so by momentum conservation the rocket gains forward momentum.
p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.explanation: The system (rocket + exhaust) has constant total momentum. Gas thrown backward has backward momentum, so the rocket must gain forward momentum. No external medium is needed.

p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.prompt: A raindrop falls through a stationary cloud of mist and gathers more mass as it falls. Why can't you simply write $mg = m\,dv/dt$ for it?
options: Because a raindrop is not subject to gravity once it is inside the cloud of mist.
Because $F=ma$ only works for rigid objects, and a growing raindrop is not rigid.
The mass is changing and the accreted mist started at rest, so $F=d(mv)/dt$ must be used.
Because the mist exerts drag that exactly cancels gravity, so the acceleration is zero.
p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.explanation: The accreted mass has to be accelerated from rest to the drop's speed; this requires momentum, which comes at the cost of the drop's acceleration. Always apply momentum balance to a well-defined system.

p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.prompt: Why can't you apply $F=ma$ directly to a body whose mass changes? Describe how to apply $F=dp/dt$ correctly to a rocket, or to a raindrop that gathers mist, and what system you must track.
p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.rubric: Full credit requires: F = ma assumes constant mass, the general law is F_ext = dp/dt for a fixed set of particles; choose a system (rocket plus the mass it will eject, or drop plus the mist it will collect) over a short time dt and compare total momentum before and after; the added or ejected mass carries its own momentum.
p1-l041-variable-mass-newton.modelAnswer: $F=ma$ holds for a fixed set of particles. For variable mass, pick a system that contains the body plus the mass about to be ejected (or captured) and compare its total momentum at $t$ and $t+dt$, including the momentum carried by that mass in your frame; then $F_{ext}=dp_{sys}/dt$.

p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.prompt: Why does dropping empty fuel tanks (staging) help a rocket reach orbital speed?
options: Empty tanks produce backward thrust, so discarding them removes a drag on the rocket.
Dropping dead mass gives the remaining stage a better mass ratio for the same exhaust speed.
The rocket equation does not apply to the first stage, so splitting it avoids the limit.
Lighter rockets have a higher exhaust speed, so each lighter stage burns more efficiently.
p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.explanation: In $\Delta v = v_{ex}\ln(m_i/m_f)$ the logarithm punishes carrying useless mass. Each stage starts with a fresh good ratio, because the structure of earlier stages is not carried along.

p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.prompt: A rocket stage burns propellant with effective exhaust speed 4.40 km/s (a typical liquid H$_2$/O$_2$ engine). What initial-to-final mass ratio $m_i/m_f$ is needed to achieve $\Delta v = 9.40$ km/s (roughly what is needed to reach low-Earth orbit), ignoring gravity and drag? Give the ratio as a pure number.
p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.explanation: $m_i/m_f = e^{\Delta v/v_{ex}} = e^{9.4/4.4} = 8.47$: about 88% of the launch mass must be propellant. The exponential is why staging matters.

p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.prompt: Outline the reasoning that gives the rocket equation, and explain in words why the final speed depends on the logarithm of the mass ratio rather than linearly on it.
p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.rubric: Full credit: apply momentum conservation over a short interval: rocket mass $m$ ejects $|dm|$ at speed $v_{ex}$ relative to the rocket so $m\,dv = v_{ex}|dm|$ (no gravity); integrate $dv = -v_{ex}\,dm/m$ to get $v_{ex}\ln(m_i/m_f)$; each fractional mass loss gives a fixed velocity increment, so equal factors in mass give equal $\Delta v$ (logarithm).
p1-l042-rocket-equation-staging.modelAnswer: In a short time the rocket (mass $m$) throws out mass $|dm|$ backward at speed $v_{ex}$ relative to itself, and momentum conservation gives $m\,dv = v_{ex}|dm|$, i.e. $dv = -v_{ex}\,dm/m$. Integrating from $m_i$ to $m_f$ yields $\Delta v = v_{ex}\ln(m_i/m_f)$. Each ejected slice of mass produces a velocity gain proportional to the fraction of the current mass it represents, so you get equal speed increments each time the mass is cut by the same factor: a logarithm.

p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.prompt: A flywheel spinning at 40.0 rad/s slows with a constant angular acceleration of -5.00 rad/s$^2$. How many complete revolutions does it make before stopping? Give the answer in revolutions.
p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.explanation: $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$ gives $\Delta\theta = 40^2/(2\cdot5) = 160$ rad $= 25.5$ rev. This is the exact analogue of $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$.

p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.prompt: A fan starts from rest and speeds up at constant angular acceleration. By the time it reaches angular speed $\omega$ it has turned through an angle $\theta$. What angle has it turned through by the time it reaches $2\omega$?
options: $4\theta$
$2\theta$
$\sqrt{2}\,\theta$
$8\theta$
p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.explanation: From $\omega^2=2\alpha\theta$ the turned angle grows as $\omega^2$, so doubling $\omega$ takes four times the angle. The rotational equations mirror $v^2=2a\,\Delta x$.

p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.prompt: Explain why the constant-angular-acceleration equations have exactly the same form as the linear constant-acceleration equations. Which rotational variable plays the role of $x$, $v$ and $a$?
p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.rubric: Full credit requires: both come from integrating a constant second derivative; the mapping theta <-> x, omega <-> v, alpha <-> a; the same algebra (including omega^2 = omega_0^2 + 2 alpha Delta theta) holds because the mathematics is identical.
p1-l043-angular-variables-constant-alpha.modelAnswer: Both sets follow from integrating a constant second derivative, so the algebra is identical with $\theta\leftrightarrow x$, $\omega\leftrightarrow v$ and $\alpha\leftrightarrow a$. That is why $\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\,\Delta\theta$ mirrors $v^2=v_0^2+2a\,\Delta x$.

p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.prompt: Two points on a rotating CD are at radii $r$ and $2r$ from the centre. Compared with the inner point, the outer point has
options: the same angular velocity and the same linear speed.
twice the angular velocity and twice the linear speed.
the same angular velocity and twice the linear speed.
half the angular velocity and the same linear speed.
p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.explanation: Every point on a rigid rotating body shares the same $\omega$ and $\alpha$ (that is why they are useful). The linear speed $v = \omega r$ grows with distance from the axis.

p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.prompt: A turntable spins at a constant angular velocity. Does a point on its rim accelerate?
options: No, because the angular velocity is constant, so nothing about the motion is changing.
Yes, with a tangential acceleration equal to $\omega r$, because the speed is nonzero.
No, because the velocity is tangent to the circle and acceleration needs a change in speed.
Yes: a centripetal acceleration $\omega^2 r$ toward the axis, but no tangential acceleration.
p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.explanation: Constant $\omega$ means $\alpha=0$ and no tangential acceleration, but the velocity vector still turns, so there is a radial acceleration $a_c=\omega^2r$.

p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.prompt: For a wheel rotating counterclockwise as seen from above, the angular velocity vector $\vec\omega$ points
options: upward along the axis (right-hand rule), so that $\vec v=\vec\omega\times\vec r$ is tangential.
downward along the axis, and the velocity of a point then points along $\vec\omega$ itself.
tangent to the rim, in the same direction as the velocity of the point on the rim.
radially outward from the axis, in the direction a loose particle would fly off.
p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.explanation: The direction of $\vec\omega$ is along the rotation axis, with sense given by curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of rotation. The cross product $\vec\omega\times\vec r$ gives the tangential velocity.

p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.prompt: Why is the radian the natural unit for angles in physics, and why do we treat angular velocity as a vector even though a rotation is not a displacement in a straight line?
p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.rubric: Full credit: the radian is defined by $s = r\theta$ (arc length per radius) so that $v=\omega r$, $a_t = \alpha r$ hold without conversion factors (derivatives of $\sin\theta$ etc.); angular velocity has a magnitude and a definite axis and sense (right-hand rule) and it relates to velocity by $\vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r$, so a vector description captures the axis.
p1-l044-angular-linear-relations-omega-v.modelAnswer: The radian is the ratio arc/radius, so $s = r\theta$, $v = \omega r$ and $a_t=\alpha r$ hold without conversion factors, and derivatives like $d(\sin\theta)/d\theta = \cos\theta$ are clean. Angular velocity specifies how fast and about which axis (and in which sense) a body turns; with the right-hand rule it behaves like a vector, and the velocity of any point is $\vec\omega\times\vec r$.

p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.prompt: A solid disk and a thin hoop have the same mass and radius and spin at the same angular velocity. Which has more rotational kinetic energy, and why?
options: The hoop, because all its mass is at the rim, so its $I=MR^2$ exceeds the disk's $\tfrac12MR^2$.
The disk, because it has more of its mass near the axis, where the material is moving fastest.
They are equal, because mass and angular velocity are the same for the two bodies.
The disk, because $I$ is larger when mass is concentrated near the centre of the body.
p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.explanation: $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ and $I = \sum m_ir_i^2$ weights mass by the square of its distance from the axis. Moving mass outward raises $I$ and hence the energy needed to spin at a given $\omega$.

p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.prompt: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its centre is $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$, but about one end it is $\tfrac13ML^2$. Why is the end value larger?
options: Because rotating about the end makes the rod heavier, which adds to its inertia.
Because the centre of mass is not at the middle of a rod, so the two axes differ.
Because the moment of inertia depends only on the total mass, not on the axis chosen.
On average the mass is farther from an end axis; the parallel-axis term $Md^2$ adds to $I_{cm}$.
p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.explanation: $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$ with $d = L/2$: $\tfrac1{12}ML^2 + \tfrac14ML^2 = \tfrac13ML^2$. Among parallel axes, the one through the centre of mass always has the smallest $I$.

p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.prompt: Explain why a hoop has a larger moment of inertia than a solid disk of the same mass and radius, and why the parallel-axis theorem always gives a larger $I$ as the axis moves away from the centre of mass.
p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.rubric: Full credit requires: I = sum m r^2 weights mass by distance squared from the axis, so mass concentrated at large radius (the hoop) gives more; the parallel-axis term M d^2 is always positive, so I is minimum about the centre of mass axis.
p1-l045-moment-of-inertia.modelAnswer: $I=\sum m_ir_i^2$ weights each piece by the square of its distance from the axis, so the hoop, with all its mass at radius $R$, exceeds the disk. In $I=I_{cm}+Md^2$ the extra term is positive, so the centre-of-mass axis always gives the smallest $I$.

p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.prompt: A mass hangs from a string wound around a pulley and falls. If the pulley is a heavy disk instead of a light one, the mass falls
options: faster, because the heavy pulley pulls harder on the string and drags the mass down.
at constant speed, because the heavier pulley balances the gravitational force exactly.
at the same rate, since the pulley does not touch the mass and cannot affect it.
more slowly, because part of the lost potential energy goes into rotating the pulley.
p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.explanation: Energy conservation: $mgh = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12I\omega^2$ with $\omega = v/R$. A larger $I$ means more of the energy is stored as rotation, so $v$ is smaller at every height.

p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.prompt: Hydrogen chloride (H$^{35}$Cl) has bond length 1.275 Angstrom. Treat it as a rigid rotor with $I = \mu r^2$ and find the rotational constant $\tilde B = \hbar/(4\pi cI)$ in cm$^{-1}$ ($m_H = 1.00783$ u, $m_{Cl} = 34.96885$ u). Give the answer in cm$^{-1}$.
p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.explanation: $\mu = 0.9796$ u $= 1.627e-27$ kg, $I = \mu r^2 = 2.644e-47$ kg m$^2$, $\tilde B = 10.59$ cm$^{-1}$ (the experimental value is about 10.6 cm$^{-1}$). A larger moment of inertia gives closer-spaced rotational levels.

p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.prompt: Explain physically what the moment of inertia measures and why, unlike mass, it depends on where the axis is placed. Then say how a heavier, longer molecule's rotational energy levels compare with those of a light, short one.
p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.rubric: Full credit: $I=\sum m_ir_i^2$ measures resistance to angular acceleration (rotational inertia), weighted by squared distance from the axis, so it depends on the mass distribution and the chosen axis; rotational energies scale as $\hbar^2/2I$, so a heavy/long molecule (large $I$) has smaller rotational constant and more closely spaced levels.
p1-l046-rotational-energy-pulleys-molecu.modelAnswer: Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass: how hard it is to change a body's rotation. Because it weights each piece of mass by $r^2$, it depends on how the mass is distributed relative to the chosen axis. In spectroscopy, rotational levels scale as $\hbar^2/2I$, so a heavy, long molecule with a large $I$ has a small rotational constant and closely spaced rotational levels.

p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.prompt: A 100 N force acts on a wheel along a line that passes exactly through the axle (the pivot). What torque does it produce about the axle?
options: 100 N m, regardless of the position.
100 N times the radius of the wheel.
Zero, because the lever arm is zero.
It depends on the angular velocity of the wheel.
p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.explanation: $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ has magnitude $rF\sin\phi$, and for a force along the line through the pivot $\phi=0$ (equivalently, lever arm = 0). Pushing straight at the hinge does not turn the door.

p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.prompt: A mechanic pulls on a 0.30 m wrench with a 80 N force that makes a $60^\circ$ angle with the wrench handle. What is the torque about the bolt? Give the answer in N m.
p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\phi = (0.30)(80)\sin60^\circ = 20.8$ N m. Only the component of the force perpendicular to the wrench ($F\sin60^\circ$) turns the bolt.

p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.prompt: State the rotational form of Newton's second law and explain each of its parts by comparison with $F = ma$, including what plays the role of force and of mass.
p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.rubric: Full credit: $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$; torque ($r\times F$, a force weighted by lever arm) replaces force, moment of inertia replaces mass (inertia depends on distribution of mass about the axis), angular acceleration replaces linear acceleration.
p1-l047-torque-rotational-second-law.modelAnswer: $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$: net torque plays the role of net force (a force's turning effect is the force times its lever arm), the moment of inertia plays the role of mass (resistance to change in rotation, depending on how mass is spread about the axis), and the angular acceleration plays the role of $a$.

p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.prompt: In a massive-pulley Atwood machine, the tensions in the string on the two sides of the pulley are different. Why?
options: The string stretches by different amounts on the two sides, giving unequal tensions.
The two masses have different weights, so each side's tension simply equals its weight.
A net torque $(T_2-T_1)R=I\alpha$ is needed to give the pulley its angular acceleration.
Tension is always larger on the side of the smaller mass, since the lighter mass resists.
p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.explanation: A pulley with rotational inertia needs a net torque to speed up its rotation. Only unequal tensions can supply it. In the massless limit $I\to0$, the tensions equalise.

p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.prompt: A motor delivers constant power. If it turns faster, what happens to the torque it delivers?
options: The torque increases, because faster motion needs a stronger twist.
The torque decreases, because $P = \tau\omega$ means $\tau = P/\omega$.
The torque stays the same, since power is constant.
The torque becomes independent of $\omega$.
p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.explanation: $P = \tau\omega$ at fixed $P$ gives an inverse relation between torque and angular speed; a car in a higher gear (higher $\omega$ of the engine for a given speed) delivers less torque to the wheels.

p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.prompt: A car engine delivers its maximum power at a high rotation rate, yet the wheels must supply a large torque to climb a hill. Using $P=\tau\omega$, explain why vehicles need gearboxes.
p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.rubric: Full credit requires: power = torque x angular speed; for a fixed available power the torque is inversely proportional to the angular speed; gears trade rotation rate for torque (like a lever trading distance for force) so the engine can run at its efficient rpm while the wheels get high torque at low speed.
p1-l048-rotational-dynamics-applications.modelAnswer: Since $P=\tau\omega$, a given power means high torque only at low rotation rate. A gear train lets the engine stay at its efficient high rpm while the wheels turn slowly with large torque, trading speed for torque much as a lever trades distance for force.

p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.prompt: A particle moves in a straight line at constant velocity, passing at a perpendicular distance $d$ from the origin. Its angular momentum $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$ about the origin is
options: zero, because the particle is not rotating about anything, so there is nothing to have angular momentum.
constant and nonzero ($L=pd$), even though the particle is not circling anything.
changing, because the angle between $\vec r$ and the path changes as the particle moves along.
zero, because no force acts on the particle and so no torque or angular momentum arises.
p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.explanation: $|\vec r\times\vec p| = p\,r\sin\phi = pd$ at every point on the line, and no torque acts (no force), so $\vec L$ is constant. Angular momentum depends on the choice of origin, not on circling.

p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.prompt: Which force produces zero torque about the origin on a particle located at position $\vec r$?
options: A force pointing along $\vec r$, toward or away from the origin
A force perpendicular to $\vec r$, if it is small enough
Any force at all, if the particle's speed is constant
A force that is constant in magnitude, whatever its direction
p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.explanation: Torque is $\vec r\times\vec F$, which vanishes only when $\vec F$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec r$. A central force therefore leaves $\vec L$ unchanged.

p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.prompt: Explain why the net torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum, how $L=I\omega$ follows for a rigid body spinning about a symmetry axis, and why $L$ is quantised in units of $\hbar$ for electrons and molecules.
p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.rubric: Full credit requires: differentiate r x p to get r x F = torque (the p x p term vanishes); for a rigid body about a symmetry axis the sum of r x m v gives I omega; in quantum mechanics orbital and rotational angular momenta come in units of hbar, so rotational energy levels depend on I (and on L^2 / 2I).
p1-l049-angular-momentum-torque.modelAnswer: Differentiating $\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p$ gives $\vec v\times\vec p=0$ plus $\vec r\times\vec F=\vec\tau$, so $d\vec L/dt=\vec\tau_{net}$. Summing $\vec r\times m\vec v$ over a rigid body about a symmetry axis gives $I\omega$. For electrons and molecules $L$ comes in units of $\hbar$, so rotational energies $L^2/2I$ are quantised and set by $I$.

p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.prompt: A spinning ice skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. What happens to her rotational kinetic energy, and why?
options: It decreases, because the moment of inertia decreased and $K$ is proportional to $I$.
It stays the same, because angular momentum is conserved and so kinetic energy cannot change either.
It increases: her muscles do positive work pulling the arms in; angular momentum stays constant.
It increases, because her angular momentum grows as she spins faster.
p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.explanation: $L = I\omega$ is conserved (no external torque), so $\omega\propto1/I$. But $K = L^2/(2I)$ grows as $I$ shrinks; the extra energy comes from her muscles doing work as she pulls her arms in.

p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.prompt: A planet orbits the Sun on an ellipse. It moves faster at perihelion (closest approach) because
options: the Sun's pull is strongest at perihelion and always speeds the planet up along its path.
the planet's mass is larger at perihelion, so its kinetic energy is larger there.
angular momentum is conserved under the Sun's central pull, so smaller $r$ means larger $v$.
friction with interplanetary gas slows the planet down on the far side of its orbit.
p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.explanation: The gravitational force on the planet is directed along the line to the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and $L$ is constant. This is Kepler's second law, equal areas in equal times.

p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.prompt: A star like the Sun's core rotates once every 25 days with radius $7.0\times10^8$ m. Suppose it collapses to a neutron star of radius $1.0\times10^4$ m, conserving mass and angular momentum, and treat both as uniform spheres ($I\propto MR^2$). What is the new rotation period? Give the answer in milliseconds.
p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.explanation: $L = I\omega$ with $I\propto R^2$ gives $\omega_2/\omega_1 = (R_1/R_2)^2 = 4.90e+09$, so $T_2 = T_1(R_2/R_1)^2 = 2.16e+06\,\mathrm{s}\times2.04e-10 = 0.44$ ms. Real pulsars rotate in milliseconds to seconds.

p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.prompt: Explain why a planet moving under a central force (like gravity) stays in a single plane and sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Use angular momentum.
p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.rubric: Full credit: central force $\parallel \vec r$ so $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F=0$ and $\vec L$ is constant in magnitude and direction; $\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p$ is always perpendicular to $\vec r$ and $\vec v$ so motion stays in the plane perpendicular to $\vec L$; area rate $dA/dt = L/2m$ is constant.
p1-l050-angular-momentum-conservation.modelAnswer: A central force points along $\vec r$, so the torque $\vec r\times\vec F$ is zero and $\vec L$ is constant. Since $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$ is perpendicular to the position vector at all times and has fixed direction, the planet moves in the plane perpendicular to $\vec L$. The area swept per unit time is $dA/dt = \tfrac12 r v_\perp = L/2m$, which is constant.

p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.prompt: A solid sphere, a solid cylinder and a hoop of identical mass and radius are released from rest at the top of an incline and roll without slipping. The finishing order (first to last) is
options: cylinder, then sphere, then hoop; the order depends on the common mass and radius.
hoop, then cylinder, then sphere, because the hoop has the largest rotational inertia.
all tie, because gravity accelerates every object equally, regardless of its shape.
sphere, then cylinder, then hoop, independent of the common mass and radius.
p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.explanation: $a = g\sin\theta/(1 + I/MR^2)$: $I/MR^2 = 2/5, 1/2, 1$ respectively. The smaller the share of energy that goes into rotation, the faster the translation. Mass and radius cancel.

p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.prompt: A solid cylinder ($I=\tfrac12MR^2$) of mass 4.0 kg rolls without slipping at 2.0 m/s. What is its total kinetic energy? Give the answer in joules.
p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.explanation: Rolling without slipping gives $\omega=v/R$, so $K=\tfrac12Mv^2+\tfrac12(\tfrac12MR^2)(v/R)^2=\tfrac34Mv^2=\tfrac34(4.0)(2.0)^2=12$ J: one third of it is rotational.

p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.prompt: When a wheel rolls without slipping at speed $v$, the contact point is instantaneously at rest and the top point moves at $2v$. Explain why, using translation plus rotation.
p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.rubric: Full credit requires: the velocity of any point is the centre velocity plus omega x r; at the bottom the rotation velocity (-omega R) cancels v_cm = omega R; at the top they add to 2 v_cm; so the contact point is the instantaneous axis of rotation and static friction does no work.
p1-l051-rolling-without-slipping.modelAnswer: Every point moves with the centre's velocity $v$ plus the rotational velocity $\omega\times r$ of size $\omega R=v$. At the bottom the rotational part points backward and cancels the translation, giving zero; at the top both point forward, giving $2v$. The contact point is the instantaneous axis, so static friction there does no work.

p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.prompt: A wheel rolls without slipping on a road. Relative to the road, the point of the wheel currently touching the ground is
options: instantaneously at rest, while the top moves at twice the centre's speed.
moving backward at speed $v_{cm}$, because the wheel's rotation carries it back along the road.
moving forward at speed $v_{cm}$, the same as the centre, because it is rigidly attached.
moving forward at twice the centre's speed, because rolling doubles the speed of every point.
p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.explanation: Velocity of a point = $\vec v_{cm} + \vec\omega\times\vec r'$. At the bottom the rotation term is $-\omega R = -v_{cm}$, cancelling $v_{cm}$; at the top it adds, giving $2v_{cm}$.

p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.prompt: A ball rolls without slipping down a rough incline. What role does static friction play, and how much mechanical energy does it dissipate?
options: It slows the ball down and converts its kinetic energy into heat at the contact point.
It is zero, because a ball that rolls without slipping feels no friction force of any kind.
It supplies the torque for spin-up but does no work, since the contact point is at rest.
It does negative work equal to $\mu_k mg\cos\theta$ times the distance rolled, heating the surfaces.
p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.explanation: Friction at the instantaneous contact point acts where the surface is stationary, so it does no work in pure rolling. It still matters: without it the ball would slide frictionlessly and not rotate at all.

p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.prompt: A solid sphere ($I = \tfrac25MR^2$) rolls without slipping down a $30^\circ$ incline. What is the acceleration of its centre? Use $g = 9.81$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in m/s$^2$.
p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.explanation: $a = g\sin\theta/(1+I/MR^2) = 9.81(0.5)/(1.4) = 3.50$ m/s$^2$, versus $4.91$ m/s$^2$ for a frictionless sliding block.

p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.prompt: Explain why a hoop loses a race down an incline to a solid sphere even though they have the same mass and radius, in terms of how the energy is shared.
p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.rubric: Full credit: total KE $=\tfrac12Mv^2 + \tfrac12I\omega^2$ with $\omega=v/R$; the hoop has larger $I/MR^2$ so a larger share of the released PE goes to rotation, leaving less in translational KE so slower $v$ at every height.
p1-l052-rolling-down-an-incline.modelAnswer: As each rolls down it converts the same potential energy $Mgh$ into kinetic energy, but this splits between the centre-of-mass motion $\tfrac12Mv^2$ and spin $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ (with $\omega = v/R$ for rolling). The hoop has the larger $I/MR^2$, so more of the energy goes into spinning and less into forward motion; it moves more slowly at every height.

p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.prompt: A spinning top is tilted off vertical. Instead of toppling over immediately, its axis slowly circles around the vertical (precession). The reason is
options: friction with the table pushes the top sideways, and that push keeps carrying its axis around in a circle.
gravity does not act on a spinning object, so nothing is left to topple it and the axis just wanders.
the spin makes the top heavier on one side, so gravity pulls that side around the vertical.
gravity's torque is perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it changes the direction of $\vec L$, not its magnitude.
p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.explanation: $d\vec L/dt = \vec\tau$ with $\vec\tau\perp\vec L$: $|\vec L|$ is constant but $\vec L$ swings around the vertical at rate $\Omega = \tau/L = mgr/I\omega$. A faster spin means a larger $L$ and slower precession.

p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.prompt: Explain qualitatively why a gyroscope's response to a force is 'sideways' (precession) and why spinning it faster slows the precession.
p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.rubric: Full credit: torque from gravity changes $\vec L$ by $d\vec L = \vec\tau dt$ along the horizontal direction perpendicular to $\vec L$, so the axis moves sideways; $\Omega=\tau/L$, so a larger $L$ (faster spin) produces a smaller change in direction per unit time.
p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.modelAnswer: The change in angular momentum is along the torque, $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$. Gravity's torque is horizontal and perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it swings the axis sideways instead of tipping it over. The rate of swing is $\Omega = \tau/L$: with larger $L$ the same torque produces a smaller change in direction, so a faster spin gives slower precession.

p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.prompt: A top spinning rapidly on its tip is slightly tilted from the vertical and precesses at a rate $\Omega$. If it is spun faster (same tilt and mass), the precession rate
options: decreases, since $\Omega=\tau/L$ and $L$ is larger
increases, since a faster spin gives a larger torque
stays the same, since gravity is unchanged
increases, since the top is more stable
p1-l053-gyroscopic-precession.explanation: Gravity's torque $\tau=mgr\sin\theta$ does not depend on the spin, while $L=I\omega$ grows with it, so the same torque turns a larger $\vec L$ more slowly: $\Omega=\tau/L$.

p1-l054-static-equilibrium.prompt: For a body in static equilibrium you may take torques about any convenient point. Why is that allowed and which point is usually smart?
options: Torque is always zero for a stationary object, so every pivot gives the same trivial equation and none is smarter.
With zero net force, torque is zero about every point if zero about one; pick a pivot on an unknown force.
Only the centre of mass is allowed as a pivot, because torque is defined about the centre of mass.
The pivot must be at the geometric centre of the body, since torque is defined from the body's centre.
p1-l054-static-equilibrium.explanation: Changing the reference point adds a term $\vec r_{shift}\times\sum\vec F$, which vanishes when the net force is zero. Choosing the pivot at an unknown force eliminates that unknown from the equation.

p1-l054-static-equilibrium.prompt: A uniform ladder leans against a smooth (frictionless) wall and is held by friction at the floor. If the ladder is made more nearly vertical (steeper), the friction needed at the floor
options: increases.
stays the same.
decreases.
becomes zero only when the ladder is horizontal.
p1-l054-static-equilibrium.explanation: Torques about the foot give $N_w L\sin\theta = \tfrac12mgL\cos\theta$, so $N_w = \tfrac12mg\cot\theta$, which is the required floor friction. Steeper (larger $\theta$ from the floor) means smaller $\cot\theta$, hence less friction.

p1-l054-static-equilibrium.prompt: Why does a ladder leaning on a smooth wall need friction at the floor? Using force and torque balance qualitatively, explain how the needed friction changes as the ladder is made steeper.
p1-l054-static-equilibrium.rubric: Full credit requires: the smooth wall pushes only horizontally so the floor friction must balance it (sum of horizontal forces zero); torque balance about the foot gives wall force proportional to the lever arm (it grows as the ladder leans out); a steeper ladder lowers the wall force and so the needed friction.
p1-l054-static-equilibrium.modelAnswer: A smooth wall can only push horizontally, so only floor friction can balance it. Torque about the foot sets that wall force: it grows as the ladder leans further from vertical, so a steeper ladder needs less friction.

p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.prompt: A 2.00 m steel wire of diameter 1.00 mm ($Y = 200$ GPa) supports a 50.0 kg mass. How much does the wire stretch? Use $g = 9.81$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in millimetres.
p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.explanation: $F = mg = 490.5$ N, $A = \pi(0.5\,\mathrm{mm})^2 = 7.854e-07$ m$^2$, stress $= 625$ MPa. $\Delta L = FL_0/(AY) = 6.25$ mm: a small strain of about 3.1e-03.

p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.prompt: Two wires of the same material and cross-section carry the same load. Wire B is twice as long as wire A. Compared with A, wire B stretches
options: twice as much
the same amount, since the stress is the same
half as much
four times as much
p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.explanation: The strain $\Delta L/L_0=F/(AY)$ is the same, so the extension $\Delta L$ is proportional to the original length $L_0$. Equivalently the stiffness $k=YA/L_0$ is halved.

p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.prompt: Explain how Young's modulus of a solid is related to the stiffness of the bonds between its atoms, and why we describe materials with stress and strain rather than force and extension.
p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.rubric: Full credit requires: the extension of a solid is the sum of many small bond stretches, each behaving like a spring; Y is the stiffness per unit area and length (k = YA/L0 for a sample); stress and strain remove dependence on the sample size so Y is a property of the material.
p1-l055-stress-strain-youngs-modulus.modelAnswer: Each atomic bond acts like a spring; the stretch of a wire is many bond stretches in series, with many chains in parallel across its area, giving $k=YA/L_0$. Using stress $F/A$ and strain $\Delta L/L_0$ removes the sample's size, so $Y$ is a material property reflecting bond stiffness.

p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.prompt: Astronauts on the International Space Station (altitude ~400 km) float freely. This is because
options: the Earth's gravity is cancelled by the Moon's pull at that altitude, leaving almost no net force.
gravity is essentially zero that high above the surface, so nothing pulls the astronauts down.
they are in continuous free fall; gravity there is still about 90% of its surface value.
the air is too thin to press them down, so they feel no weight at that altitude.
p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.explanation: At 400 km up, $g \approx 8.7$ m/s$^2$. The station and its occupants fall together, orbiting fast enough that they continually 'miss' the Earth, so there is no contact force and they feel weightless.

p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.prompt: What is the free-fall acceleration at the altitude of the International Space Station, 400 km above the surface? Use $g_0 = 9.81$ m/s$^2$ at the surface and $R_E = 6371$ km. Give the answer in m/s$^2$.
p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.explanation: $g(h) = g_0\left(\frac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2 = 9.81(6371/6771)^2 = 8.69$ m/s$^2$ (the linear approximation $g_0(1-2h/R_E) = 8.58$ is already off because $h/R$ is not tiny).

p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.prompt: State Newton's law of gravitation in words, explain how $g=GM/R^2$ follows for a planet, and say why weight decreases only slightly (by $2h/R$) at altitudes small compared with the planet's radius.
p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.rubric: Full credit requires: attractive force proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of separation; surface g from F = mg = GMm/R^2 (so g is independent of m); expansion (1+h/R)^-2 ~ 1 - 2h/R gives only a small fractional change for h << R.
p1-l056-universal-gravitation-surface-gr.modelAnswer: The force is attractive, proportional to $m_1m_2$ and to $1/r^2$. Setting $mg=GMm/R^2$ gives $g=GM/R^2$ independent of $m$. At height $h$, $g=g_0(1+h/R)^{-2}\approx g_0(1-2h/R)$, a small correction for $h\ll R$.

p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.prompt: Assume the Earth were a uniform ball. How would the gravitational acceleration at half the Earth's radius (inside) compare with its surface value?
options: Half, because only the mass inside radius $r$ attracts: $g\propto r$ inside a uniform ball.
The same as at the surface, because the enclosed mass shrinks exactly as the distance does.
Zero, because the shell of matter outside the point cancels everything, including the inner part.
Four times larger, since gravity follows $1/r^2$ and the distance to the centre is halved.
p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.explanation: By the shell theorem, outer shells exert no net force; the enclosed mass is $M(r/R)^3$, so $g = G M (r/R)^3/r^2 = GMr/R^3$: linear in $r$ inside, and zero at the centre.

p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.prompt: Gravity is about $10^{36}$ times weaker than the electrostatic force between two protons, yet gravity dominates the motion of planets and galaxies. Why?
options: Because gravity becomes stronger than the electric force once the distances are astronomically large.
Bulk matter is electrically neutral so electric forces cancel, but gravity only attracts and adds up.
Because electric forces are completely shielded by the empty space between planets and stars.
Because planets and stars contain no charged particles, so no electric force can arise at all.
p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.explanation: Positive and negative charges nearly cancel in bulk matter, leaving almost no net electric force at large scales. Gravity has only one sign, so every particle adds to it. In chemistry the opposite is true: at molecular scales the electrostatic interaction wins.

p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.prompt: State Newton's shell theorem and use it to explain why gravity grows linearly with distance from the centre inside a uniform planet but falls off as one over r squared outside it.
p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.rubric: Full credit: a uniform spherical shell attracts outside bodies as if its mass were at the centre and exerts no net force on a body inside it; so inside at radius $r$ only the enclosed mass $M(r/R)^3$ pulls (as if at centre), giving $g\propto r$; outside, all of $M$ acts as if at centre giving $GM/r^2$.
p1-l057-shell-theorem-gravity-vs-electro.modelAnswer: The shell theorem says a uniform spherical shell attracts external bodies as though all its mass were at its centre and exerts no net force on anything inside. Outside the planet, all mass acts from the centre, so $g = GM/r^2$. Inside at radius $r$, only the mass within $r$, $M(r/R)^3$, matters, so $g = GM r/R^3$, growing linearly with $r$ from zero at the centre.

p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.prompt: A satellite in a low circular orbit loses energy to atmospheric drag. What happens to its orbital speed as it spirals inward?
options: It increases: the total energy $-GMm/2r$ falls as $r$ shrinks, while $K=GMm/2r$ rises.
It decreases, since drag is a backward force that takes kinetic energy from the satellite.
It stays the same, because a circular orbit has a fixed speed regardless of its radius.
It decreases to zero, and then the satellite falls straight down toward the planet.
p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.explanation: For circular orbits $K = GMm/2r$ and $U = -GMm/r$. Drag removes total energy, the orbit shrinks, and the speed $\sqrt{GM/r}$ rises. The work done by gravity on the inward spiral exceeds drag's removal of $K$.

p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.prompt: What is the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit 400 km above the Earth's surface? Use $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$/kg$^2$, $M_E = 5.972\times10^{24}$ kg, $R_E = 6371$ km. Give the answer in km/s.
p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.explanation: $v = \sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{(6.674\times10^{-11})(5.972\times10^{24})/(6.771\times10^6)} = 7.67$ km/s, about 27,600 km/h; the period is ~92 min.

p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.prompt: Why do we choose the gravitational potential energy to be zero at infinite separation, and what does the sign of the total energy of a satellite tell you?
p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.rubric: Full credit: $U=-GMm/r$ follows from integrating the inverse-square force from infinity (natural reference since force vanishes there); with that choice negative total energy means the object cannot reach infinity (bound), positive means unbound, zero is the escape borderline; energy needed to escape equals $-E$.
p1-l058-gravitational-potential-energy-c.modelAnswer: Integrating the inverse-square force from infinity inward gives $U(r) = -GMm/r$; infinity is a natural zero because the force vanishes there. With that convention, $E<0$ means the object lacks the energy to reach infinity (a bound orbit), $E>0$ means it can escape, and the magnitude of a negative $E$ is the binding energy, the energy needed to free it.

p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.prompt: A satellite moves from one circular orbit to a larger circular orbit using a Hohmann transfer. Compared with the initial orbit, the satellite's final speed and total energy are
options: higher speed and higher total energy.
lower speed and higher (less negative) total energy.
lower speed and lower total energy.
higher speed and lower total energy.
p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.explanation: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ falls with $r$, while $E = -GMm/2r$ increases toward zero. The engine burns put in energy, which is traded into potential energy; kinetic energy is actually smaller in the bigger orbit.

p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.prompt: A spacecraft's total energy (kinetic plus gravitational, with $U\to0$ at infinity) is positive. Its path is
options: a hyperbola: the spacecraft is unbound and escapes to infinity with speed to spare.
a circle with a very large radius, because a larger orbit has more energy than a small one.
an ellipse; it is bound to the planet, though its orbit may be very large.
a spiral that eventually returns to the planet, because positive energy leaks away into heat.
p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.explanation: $E<0$ means bound (ellipse or circle); $E=0$ is the parabolic borderline (escape with zero leftover speed at infinity); $E>0$ means hyperbolic and unbound. Setting $U(\infty)=0$ makes the sign of $E$ meaningful.

p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.prompt: A Hohmann transfer to a higher circular orbit needs two engine burns, yet the satellite ends up moving more slowly than before. Explain why, and what happened to its total energy.
p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.rubric: Full credit requires: the first burn raises apoapsis (adds energy and speed at periapsis); the second burn at apoapsis speeds it up to circularise; in the higher circular orbit v = sqrt(GM/r) is smaller, kinetic energy is lower but potential energy is higher by more, so the total energy E = -GMm/2r has increased.
p1-l059-orbital-energy-classification-tr.modelAnswer: The first burn speeds the satellite up to enter an ellipse whose far point touches the higher orbit; the second burn there raises its speed enough to circularise. In the larger circle $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ is smaller, but total energy $-GMm/2r$ has risen (become less negative), because potential energy rose by more than kinetic energy fell.

p1-l060-keplers-laws.prompt: A comet moves much faster near perihelion than near aphelion. Which principle explains this directly?
options: The comet gets heavier near the Sun, which gives it more momentum and so a larger speed.
Conservation of the comet's linear momentum, which keeps its speed fixed along the path.
Kepler's third law, which relates the comet's period to the semi-major axis of its orbit.
Conservation of angular momentum: $r v_\perp$ is constant, so smaller $r$ means larger $v$.
p1-l060-keplers-laws.explanation: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) is angular momentum conservation, and holds for any central force. Energy conservation gives the same speeds when you know the potential, but it is the angular momentum that links $v$ and $r$ here.

p1-l060-keplers-laws.prompt: Two stars orbit their common centre of mass. If the total mass of the pair doubles while their separation stays the same, the orbital period
options: doubles.
decreases by a factor of $\sqrt2$.
stays the same.
decreases by a factor of 2.
p1-l060-keplers-laws.explanation: Kepler's third law for a binary: $T^2 = 4\pi^2a^3/G(M_1+M_2)$, so $T\propto(M_1+M_2)^{-1/2}$. More mass means stronger gravity, so the orbit is traversed faster.

p1-l060-keplers-laws.prompt: Halley's comet has a semi-major axis of 17.8 AU. Using Kepler's third law in solar units ($T$ in years, $a$ in AU, $T^2 = a^3$), what is its orbital period? Give the answer in years.
p1-l060-keplers-laws.explanation: $T = a^{3/2} = 17.8^{1.5} = 75.1$ years, matching the observed ~76-year return interval (the small difference comes from planetary perturbations and rounding).

p1-l060-keplers-laws.prompt: Explain why Kepler's second law (equal areas) holds for any central force but Kepler's third law (T squared proportional to a cubed) depends on the force being an inverse-square law.
p1-l060-keplers-laws.rubric: Full credit: central force has zero torque so $L$ constant so $dA/dt = L/2m$ constant regardless of force law; for a circular orbit with $F=GMm/r^2$: $mv^2/r = GMm/r^2$ and $T=2\pi r/v$ gives $T^2 = 4\pi^2 r^3/GM$; a different force law gives a different scaling of $T$ with $r$.
p1-l060-keplers-laws.modelAnswer: The area law comes only from zero torque (a central force), so it applies to any force law. For the third law, set the inverse-square force equal to $mv^2/r$ to get $v^2 = GM/r$, and with $T = 2\pi r/v$ obtain $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$. A different dependence of force on $r$ would yield a different relation between $T$ and $r$.

p1-l061-tidal-forces.prompt: Tides on Earth come from the Moon's gravity. The reason there are two tidal bulges (one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side) is that
options: the Moon pulls the near side of the Earth and pushes the far side away from itself, making two bulges.
the Earth's rotation flings water outward on the side facing away from the Moon, making the second bulge.
the Moon's pull differs across the Earth, stretching it: strongest on the near side, weakest on the far side.
the Sun pulls the far side of the Earth while the Moon pulls the near side, making two bulges.
p1-l061-tidal-forces.explanation: Relative to the Earth's centre, the near side is pulled toward the Moon and the far side is left behind (pulled less), stretching the Earth along the Earth-Moon line. Tides are a field-gradient effect, scaling like $1/r^3$.

p1-l061-tidal-forces.prompt: Estimate the difference in the Moon's gravitational acceleration between the near and far sides of the Earth's centre, $\Delta g\approx 2GM_{Moon}R_E/d^3$. Use $M_{Moon}=7.342\times10^{22}$ kg, $R_E=6.371\times10^{6}$ m, $d=3.844\times10^{8}$ m, $G=6.674\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$/kg$^2$. Give the answer in m/s$^2$.
p1-l061-tidal-forces.explanation: $\Delta g\approx 2(6.674\times10^{-11})(7.342\times10^{22})(6.371\times10^6)/(3.844\times10^8)^3 = 1.1\times10^{-6}$ m/s$^2$, about a ten-millionth of $g$, yet enough to raise the oceans by about a metre.

p1-l061-tidal-forces.prompt: Explain what a tidal force is in terms of the difference in gravitational pull across an extended body, and why it falls off as $1/d^3$ rather than $1/d^2$.
p1-l061-tidal-forces.rubric: Full credit requires: the field differs between the near and far parts of the body, so relative to its centre the near side is pulled more toward the source and the far side less (stretching along the line, squeezing across it); the difference is the derivative of GM/d^2 times the body's size, giving ~ 1/d^3.
p1-l061-tidal-forces.modelAnswer: Each part of the body feels a slightly different pull; relative to the centre, the near side is pulled more strongly and the far side less, which stretches the body along the line to the source. That difference is the gradient $d(GM/d^2)/dd\times R\sim 2GMR/d^3$, so it falls off as $1/d^3$.

p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.prompt: A mass on an ideal spring oscillates with amplitude $A$. If the amplitude is doubled, the period
options: is halved.
doubles.
stays the same.
increases by a factor of $\sqrt2$.
p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.explanation: $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ depends only on the spring and the mass. Larger amplitude means larger speeds that exactly compensate the longer path, so the period is independent of amplitude (isochronism of SHM).

p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.prompt: A mass oscillates with $x(t)=0.12\cos(5.0t+0.50)$ in metres (with $t$ in seconds). What is its maximum speed? Give the answer in m/s.
p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.explanation: Differentiating, $v=-A\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi)$, so the maximum speed is $A\omega=(0.12)(5.0)=0.60$ m/s. The phase 0.50 rad only shifts when this happens.

p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.prompt: Explain why a restoring force proportional to the displacement, $F=-kx$, leads to sinusoidal motion whose period does not depend on the amplitude. How is the motion related to uniform circular motion?
p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.rubric: Full credit: $m\ddot x = -kx$ means acceleration is proportional and opposite to displacement, solved by $x = A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ with $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ fixed by $k$ and $m$ only (amplitude is a free constant, since the equation is linear); SHM is the projection (shadow) of uniform circular motion on a diameter, the circle of radius $A$ with angular speed $\omega$.
p1-l062-shm-equation-of-motion.modelAnswer: The equation $m\ddot x=-kx$ is linear, and its solutions are $x=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ with $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ set by the system alone while the amplitude $A$ is arbitrary, so the period doesn't depend on $A$. The motion is the shadow on a diameter of a point moving uniformly around a circle of radius $A$ with angular speed $\omega$: maximum speed $A\omega$ at the centre, zero at the ends.

p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.prompt: During SHM, where along the motion are the kinetic energy and potential energy each at a maximum?
options: Kinetic energy is greatest at the turning points and potential energy greatest at equilibrium.
Both are constant throughout the motion, because the total energy of the system is constant.
Both are at their maximum at the equilibrium position, since that is where the speed is highest.
Kinetic energy is greatest at equilibrium, potential energy greatest at the turning points.
p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.explanation: $E = \tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12kx^2$. At $x=0$ all of the energy is kinetic; at $x=\pm A$ the particle is momentarily at rest and all is potential. Energy sloshes between the two forms twice per period.

p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.prompt: Replacing hydrogen by deuterium in a C-H bond leaves the force constant essentially unchanged but doubles the (approximate) reduced mass. The stretching wavenumber in the IR spectrum therefore
options: doubles.
is unchanged, because the bond is the same.
decreases by a factor of about $\sqrt2$.
increases by a factor of $\sqrt2$.
p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.explanation: $\tilde\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi c}\sqrt{k/\mu}\propto\mu^{-1/2}$. The electron distribution (which sets $k$) is nearly identical for the isotopes, so heavier D gives a lower frequency, a standard IR check for assignments.

p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.prompt: The CO molecule has bond force constant $k = 1857$ N/m and reduced mass $\mu = 6.857$ u. Find the vibrational wavenumber $\tilde\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi c}\sqrt{k/\mu}$ in cm$^{-1}$. ($1$ u $= 1.6605\times10^{-27}$ kg.) Give the answer in cm$^{-1}$.
p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.explanation: $\mu = 1.138e-26$ kg, $\omega = \sqrt{k/\mu} = 4.039e+14$ rad/s, $\tilde\nu = 2144$ cm$^{-1}$, close to the observed 2143 cm$^{-1}$ IR band of CO (the small difference reflects anharmonicity).

p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.prompt: Describe how the kinetic and potential energies of a mass on a spring trade places during one cycle, why the total depends on the square of the amplitude, and what this implies for the vibrational frequency when an atom in a bond is replaced by a heavier isotope.
p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.rubric: Full credit requires: K and U exchange (K maximum at equilibrium, U maximum at turning points) with constant sum (1/2) k A^2; amplitude squared because both energies are quadratic; heavier isotope means larger reduced mass at the same k, so omega = sqrt(k/mu) and the IR wavenumber decrease.
p1-l063-shm-energy-molecular-vibrations.modelAnswer: Energy alternates between kinetic (largest at equilibrium) and potential (largest at the turning points) while the sum $\tfrac12kA^2$ stays constant, scaling with $A^2$ because both forms are quadratic. A heavier isotope raises the reduced mass at the same force constant, so $\omega=\sqrt{k/\mu}$ and the IR wavenumber fall.

p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.prompt: A simple pendulum swings with a small amplitude. If the mass of the bob is doubled (same string, same amplitude), the period
options: is unchanged, since the gravitational force and the inertia both scale with the mass.
doubles, because a heavier bob has more inertia and so takes longer to swing back and forth.
is halved, because a heavier bob is pulled down harder and so swings through faster.
increases by a factor of $\sqrt2$, as it would for a spring whose attached mass is doubled.
p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.explanation: The restoring force is $mg\sin\theta$ and the inertia is $m$, so $m$ cancels in $\ddot\theta = -(g/L)\sin\theta$. This independence of mass reflects the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass (Galileo).

p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.prompt: A simple pendulum is released from rest at an angle of $60^\circ$ from the vertical. Its exact period is how many times the small-angle period $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$? (The exact ratio is $\frac{2}{\pi}K(\sin^2(\theta_0/2))$ with $K$ the complete elliptic integral of the first kind.) Give the ratio as a pure number.
p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.explanation: The ratio is 1.0732: at $60^\circ$ the period is about 7% longer than the small-angle formula, because the restoring force $mg\sin\theta$ is weaker than the linear approximation $mg\theta$.

p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.prompt: The pendulum equation is $\ddot\theta=-(g/L)\sin\theta$. Explain what approximation turns it into simple harmonic motion, why it is reasonable, and what happens to the period when the swing becomes large.
p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.rubric: Full credit: for small $\theta$ (radians), $\sin\theta\approx\theta$, so $\ddot\theta = -(g/L)\theta$, a linear restoring torque, giving SHM with $\omega=\sqrt{g/L}$; at larger amplitude $\sin\theta<\theta$ so the restoring force is weaker than the linear model and the period increases with amplitude.
p1-l064-simple-pendulum-small-angle.modelAnswer: For small angles measured in radians, $\sin\theta\approx\theta$, which makes the restoring term linear and gives SHM with $\omega=\sqrt{g/L}$ and a period independent of amplitude. For large swings $\sin\theta$ is less than $\theta$, so the restoring torque is weaker than the linear model predicts and the pendulum takes longer to complete a swing: the period grows with amplitude.

p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.prompt: A torsional pendulum (a disk hanging from a twisting wire) has a period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$. If the disk's moment of inertia is quadrupled, the period
options: quadruples.
stays the same.
doubles.
is halved.
p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.explanation: For torsion the restoring torque is $-\kappa\theta$ (exactly linear), so the equation is $I\ddot\theta = -\kappa\theta$; $T\propto\sqrt I$. Unlike the gravity pendulum, a torsion pendulum is isochronous for all amplitudes (within the elastic limit).

p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.prompt: A uniform rod of length $L$ is pivoted at one end and swings as a physical pendulum ($I=\tfrac13ML^2$, $d=L/2$). Compared with a simple pendulum of the same length $L$, its period is
options: shorter by a factor of $\sqrt{1/3}$, because the moment of inertia is one third of $ML^2$.
longer, since the mass of a rod is spread out and so is on average farther from the pivot.
the same, since the length of the rod equals the length of the string in the simple pendulum.
shorter, by a factor $\sqrt{2/3}$: it behaves like a simple pendulum of length $2L/3$.
p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.explanation: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(Mgd)} = 2\pi\sqrt{(\tfrac13ML^2)/(Mg\tfrac L2)} = 2\pi\sqrt{2L/3g}$. The mass is on average closer to the pivot than the end, giving a smaller effective length.

p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.prompt: Explain why the period of a physical pendulum depends on both its moment of inertia and the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass, and why a uniform rod pivoted at one end swings like a simple pendulum of length $2L/3$.
p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.rubric: Full credit requires: restoring torque is mgd sin(theta) while inertia against rotation is I, giving T = 2 pi sqrt(I/(mgd)); for a rod I = (1/3)ML^2 and d = L/2 so T = 2 pi sqrt(2L/(3g)), equal to the simple pendulum with L_eq = 2L/3.
p1-l065-physical-torsional-pendulums.modelAnswer: The restoring torque is $mgd\sin\theta$ and the resistance to angular acceleration is $I$, so $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$. For a uniform rod pivoted at its end $I=\tfrac13ML^2$ and $d=L/2$, giving $T=2\pi\sqrt{2L/(3g)}$: the same as a simple pendulum of length $2L/3$.

p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.prompt: A damped oscillator (door closer, shock absorber) should return to equilibrium as fast as possible without overshooting. Which damping regime is ideal?
options: Critical damping.
Underdamping (several oscillations).
Overdamping with very strong friction.
No damping.
p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.explanation: Critical damping ($b = 2\sqrt{km}$) returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating. Overdamping also does not oscillate but creeps back more slowly; underdamping overshoots.

p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.prompt: A mass of 0.200 kg on a spring with $k = 80.0$ N/m has a damping coefficient $b = 0.0500$ kg/s. Find its quality factor $Q = \omega_0 m/b$. Give the answer as a pure number.
p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.explanation: $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m} = 20.0$ rad/s, so $Q = (20.0)(0.200)/0.0500 = 80$. The energy decays by a factor $e$ in $Q/\omega_0 = 4.0$ s, which is about $Q/2\pi \approx 13$ oscillations, and the resonance width is $\omega_0/Q =0.25$ rad/s.

p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.prompt: Describe the three damping regimes of $m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0$ and explain what the quality factor $Q$ tells you about how many oscillations occur before the energy has decayed appreciably.
p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.rubric: Full credit requires: underdamped (oscillation under a decaying envelope), critically damped (fastest non-oscillatory return), overdamped (slow monotonic return); Q is roughly 2 pi times energy stored over energy lost per cycle, so high Q means many oscillations (about Q/2 pi cycles per e-fold of energy).
p1-l066-damped-oscillations-quality-fact.modelAnswer: Underdamped systems oscillate inside a decaying envelope, critically damped ones return to rest fastest without oscillating, and overdamped ones creep back slowly. $Q=\omega_0m/b$ measures energy stored per energy lost per radian, so a high-$Q$ system rings for many cycles before its energy decays.

p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.prompt: Reducing the damping of a driven oscillator (e.g., a higher-Q spectral resonance) makes the resonance peak
options: shorter and broader.
taller and broader.
shifted but with the same height and width.
taller and narrower.
p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.explanation: At resonance the amplitude is limited by damping: $A_{max}\approx F_0/(b\omega_0)$. The width is $\Delta\omega\approx b/m = \omega_0/Q$. Lower $b$ raises $Q$, increasing height and narrowing the band.

p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.prompt: A driven damped oscillator is pushed at a frequency far below its natural frequency, $\omega\ll\omega_0$. In steady state the displacement
options: follows the driving force in phase, with a small amplitude about $F_0/k$.
lags the force by 90 degrees with a very large amplitude.
is opposite in phase to the force with amplitude much smaller than $F_0/k$.
is zero, since the system cannot respond at that frequency.
p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.explanation: Very slow driving just moves the system quasi-statically: $kx\approx F(t)$, so $x$ is in phase with $F$ with amplitude $F_0/k$. Near resonance the phase lag is $90^\circ$ and far above it the displacement is opposite to the force.

p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.prompt: Explain what the quality factor Q tells you about a damped oscillator and how it is connected to the width of a spectral line (such as an NMR or IR resonance).
p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.rubric: Full credit: $Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega$ is large for weak damping; it counts roughly how many oscillations occur before the energy decays (about $Q/2\pi$); a system that rings for many cycles responds only to a narrow band of driving frequencies so the resonance (spectral line) is narrow with width $\approx\omega_0/Q = b/m$; short-lived (strongly damped) states give broad lines.
p1-l067-driven-oscillations-resonance.modelAnswer: $Q = \omega_0 m/b$ measures how weakly damped the oscillator is: roughly $Q/2\pi$ oscillations occur before the energy falls to $1/e$. A system that rings for a long time responds only to drive frequencies very close to $\omega_0$, so its resonance is narrow, with full width about $\omega_0/Q$. In spectroscopy the same relation links the lifetime of an excited state to its linewidth: long-lived states give sharp lines and short-lived (strongly damped) ones give broad lines.

p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.prompt: Three containers of different shapes (a wide tank, a narrow tube, and a funnel) are filled with water to the same height. The pressure at the bottom of each is
options: largest in the narrow tube, because all the water is concentrated in a small space.
largest in the wide tank, because it holds the most water pressing down on the bottom.
the same, because it depends only on depth and fluid density, not on the container shape.
smallest in the funnel, because the funnel's sloping sides carry part of the water's weight.
p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.explanation: $p = p_0 + \rho gh$ follows from balancing the weight of a column of fluid. The shape of the container is irrelevant: the fluid pressure at a point depends on depth (the hydrostatic paradox).

p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.prompt: What is the total (absolute) pressure at a depth of 10.0 m in fresh water, given atmospheric pressure of 101325 Pa? Use $\rho = 1000$ kg/m$^3$ and $g = 9.81$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in atmospheres.
p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.explanation: $p = p_0 + \rho gh = 101325 + (1000)(9.81)(10.0) = 199425$ Pa $= 1.968$ atm. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere, which is why divers feel pressure so quickly.

p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.prompt: Explain why pressure in a static fluid increases linearly with depth, and what the difference is between absolute and gauge pressure.
p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.rubric: Full credit requires: the fluid layer at a given depth must support the weight of the fluid above it per unit area (p = p0 + rho g h); pressure acts equally in all directions and does not depend on container shape; gauge pressure is the excess over atmospheric pressure, absolute includes it.
p1-l068-pressure-hydrostatics.modelAnswer: A layer of fluid must hold up the weight of all the fluid above it per unit area, so $p=p_0+\rho gh$, increasing linearly with depth and acting equally in all directions. Gauge pressure is the part above atmospheric ($\rho gh$); absolute pressure includes the atmosphere.

p1-l069-pascal-archimedes.prompt: An ice cube floats in a glass filled to the brim with water. When the ice melts completely, the water level
options: stays the same (nothing overflows).
falls, because ice shrinks when it melts.
rises, so water spills out.
falls only if the ice is cold enough.
p1-l069-pascal-archimedes.explanation: A floating object displaces water of weight equal to its own weight. When it melts, the water it becomes has exactly the same weight, hence the same volume as the displaced water. (Melting land ice, in contrast, does raise sea level.)

p1-l069-pascal-archimedes.prompt: A hydraulic lift multiplies force by 100 (area ratio 100:1). Why doesn't this violate energy conservation?
options: The fluid creates the extra energy, since pressure in the fluid can be converted into work.
The small piston moves 100 times farther, so the work in equals the work out.
Pressure is not conserved in fluids, so the output force can exceed the input force freely.
The large piston has more mass, so it stores the extra energy as gravitational potential energy.
p1-l069-pascal-archimedes.explanation: Pascal's principle transmits pressure, so $F_2 = F_1(A_2/A_1)$. Incompressibility ensures equal volumes displaced: $A_1d_1 = A_2d_2$. Thus $F_1d_1 = F_2d_2$: a force multiplier trades distance for force.
